With the veteran operators, we say a dependable crew looks after its own. Supervisors hear that backing the schedule shows they can keep the floor orderly. It is one proposal, but the reason to support it can feel personal.

Interviewer: The conveyor would be stopped for 90 minutes, while the other line runs and an alternate aisle stays available. The work is estimated at $3,100.

Venn: Those are the details. But a meeting can become a spreadsheet, and people leave without deciding. I want them to picture the person beside them on a late shift, or the team they have built over years. If someone objects, we ask whether they really want coworkers to shoulder avoidable worry just to protect a short stretch of routine. Nobody wants to be the person who put convenience ahead of the crew.

Interviewer: Even though the reported stumble caused no injury?

Venn: Of course. We are asking for support before a small concern becomes the kind of thing people remember for the wrong reason.
